story.title: Susan Smith Denied Parole Again After 32 Years for Drowning Her Sons
story.summary: Susan Smith has been denied parole for the second time in two years, 32 years after she drowned her two sons in a South Carolina lake. During the hearing, Smith expressed regret and stated that her children 'did not deserve to die.' She was sentenced to life in prison for the 1994 drownings of 3-year-old Michael and 14-month-old Alex.

explore_lenses.label: Why was Smith eligible for parole at all?
explore_lenses.title: Her 1994 sentence remained parole-eligible
explore_lenses.summary: Smith received two life sentences for the 1994 murders, but the sentencing law applicable to her case permitted parole consideration after 30 years. Eligibility required a hearing; it did not create a right to release.

claims.text: South Carolina corrections records list Smith as serving two active life sentences for murder, with a projected parole-eligibility date of November 20, 2026 and no projected release date.
Associated Press reporting says the law in effect when Smith was sentenced allowed her to seek parole after 30 years and, after a denial, every two years.
South Carolina's parole guidance says the board must assess evidence of reform, likely future law-abiding conduct, the interests of society, and a suitable employment plan before granting parole.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after this denial?
explore_lenses.title: The next ordinary review is two years away
explore_lenses.summary: The denial keeps Smith incarcerated, but it does not end her parole eligibility. State procedure calls for a new hearing for violent-offense prisoners two years after a rejection, while each hearing is decided independently.

claims.text: South Carolina parole criteria state that a person serving time for a violent offense is reheard two years after a parole rejection, subject to applicable legal exceptions.
The agency's parole guide likewise says inmates denied parole for violent offenses are considered again every two years.
Board policy says a denial must be accompanied by written reasons and the date of the next hearing, and that prior decisions do not bind later parole hearings.

story_report.summary: Susan Smith has again been denied parole, 32 years after her conviction for drowning her two sons in 1994. At the hearing, Smith expressed regret, saying her children did not deserve to die. The decision means she will remain in prison, where South Carolina records list her as serving two active life sentences for murder and no projected release date.

sections.heading: Smith's Sentence and Parole Status
sections.body: South Carolina corrections records list Smith's projected parole-eligibility date as Nov. 20, 2026, while also showing no projected release date. Associated Press reporting says the law in effect when she was sentenced permitted a parole request after 30 years and allowed further consideration every two years following a denial.

sections.heading: South Carolina Parole Review Rules
sections.body: Under South Carolina parole criteria, people imprisoned for violent offenses are generally reheard two years after parole is rejected, subject to legal exceptions. The parole board evaluates evidence of reform, the likelihood of future law-abiding conduct, society's interests and an applicant's employment plan. Board policy requires written reasons for a denial and notice of the next hearing date, while specifying that earlier decisions do not control later hearings.

unresolved.text: The board's written reasons for Smith's latest parole denial were not located in the reviewed materials.
The two-year review rule suggests 2028 as the ordinary timing for another hearing, but the reviewed sources do not establish a scheduled date or indicate the result of any future application.
